components.title: Customer Identity Services
components.description: Assessment coverage provided by nobytes.compliance collectors and nobytes_cca evaluators for customer-identity-services. This document asserts what is ASSESSED, not what is implemented.

control-implementations.description: Controls this component can produce evidence for. A control absent from this list is not assessed on this platform.

implemented-requirements.description: Customers are not authenticated by the corporate directory. Customer identity almost always lives in a separate estate -- a B2C tenant, a bespoke portal, or a provider's platform -- which is outside the inventory this project assesses. Answering it from the corporate tenant would describe staff, not customers, and would be wrong in the direction that matters: it would report a pass.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The service catalogue entry for each online customer service handling sensitive customer data, recording the customer authentication design and the date it was last reviewed.

props.name: attestation-owner
props.value: Product owner for each customer-facing service

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: Customer identity is a separate estate from the corporate directory this project inventories, and is frequently operated by a provider. Deriving a verdict from corporate identity data would answer a different question about a different population of people.

statements.description: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate customers to online customer services that process, store or communicate sensitive customer data.

implemented-requirements.remarks: Residual assessment gap: Customers are not authenticated by the corporate directory. components.title: Entra Id Tenant
components.description: Assessment coverage provided by nobytes.compliance collectors and nobytes_cca evaluators for entra-id-tenant. This document asserts what is ASSESSED, not what is implemented.

control-implementations.description: Controls this component can produce evidence for. A control absent from this list is not assessed on this platform.

implemented-requirements.description: Observes that the tenant REQUIRES a second factor, from an enforcing conditional access policy covering all users and all resources. Three residual gaps are stated rather than papered over. A policy is configuration, not evidence that any sign-in actually presented a second factor. The control scopes to services that process, store or communicate sensitive data, and the tenant does not record which of its services those are -- so "all resources" is used as the conservative proxy and a narrower, correctly-scoped policy would read here as a near miss. And every real tenant excludes break-glass accounts, so exclusions are counted against a threshold rather than forbidden; the threshold is a judgement, not an observation.

implemented-requirements.description: Observes which authentication methods the TENANT POLICY enables, which is a statement about what users may register -- not about what any user actually registered or presented at a sign-in. The control speaks to what multi-factor authentication "uses", and the gap between enabled and used is real: a tenant may permit only acceptable methods while a given account holds none of them. Closing it needs sign-in logs, which is PR 10's evidence-provider work. Factor STRENGTH is deliberately out of scope here; phishing resistance is an ML2/ML3 bar under a different control.

statements.description: Multi-factor authentication uses either: something people have and something people know, or something people have that is unlocked by something people know or are.

implemented-requirements.description: Verifies MacroRuntimeScanScope is set to scan macros, which is how Office hands macro content to AMSI. implemented-requirements.description: Verifies the ADMX policy state that implements the block, in machine scope and in every loaded user policy hive. A pass here means macros are disabled, not that the exemption process is sound; a fail may be a legitimately approved exemption.

components.title: Privileged Access Process
components.description: Assessment coverage provided by nobytes.compliance collectors and nobytes_cca evaluators for privileged-access-process. This document asserts what is ASSESSED, not what is implemented.

control-implementations.description: Controls this component can produce evidence for. A control absent from this list is not assessed on this platform.

implemented-requirements.description: The control is about an act of validation at a moment in the past, not about a system's current state. A directory can show that an account holds privilege; it cannot show that the request for it was validated, by whom, or against what criteria. Group membership is not evidence of approval -- treating it as such is precisely how an unapproved administrator comes to be reported as compliant.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: Privileged access request records in the service management system, showing for each grant the requester, the validating authority and the date, held for the retention period required by the agency's record-keeping policy.

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: The evidence is an approval record, not a system state. Even a perfectly instrumented directory records only the resulting membership, and a membership that exists today says nothing about whether its request was validated when it was first made.

statements.description: Requests for privileged access to systems and their resources are validated when first requested.

implemented-requirements.remarks: Residual assessment gap: The control is about an act of validation at a moment in the past, not about a system's current state. A directory can show that an account holds privilege; it cannot show that the request for it was validated, by whom, or against what criteria. Group membership is not evidence of approval -- treating it as such is precisely how an unapproved administrator comes to be reported as compliant.

implemented-requirements.description:
The control compares two quantities and neither is a system state, which is what separates it from the four other privileged-access controls examined alongside it and deferred rather than attested.
"Explicitly authorised to access online services" is an approval. A security group, a proxy rule or an Entra group is the *implementation* of an authorisation decision, never the decision -- the same substitution this project already refused for ism-1507. Here it cuts deeper: for ism-1507 the approval merely produces a membership the control is about, while here the approval *defines the population the control is a statement about*, so a directory read cannot even compute the denominator.
"Only what is required for users to undertake their duties or functions" is a proportionality judgement about a person's job. No directory, PAM vault, identity governance platform, proxy or CASB holds an attribute meaning "what this person's duties require". An access review records that an approver clicked approve, which returns you to the first term. A job title is a string, not a set of required services.
What settles it is that no product implements "strictly limited to what is required" the way a conditional access policy implements "MFA is required". Where such a mechanism exists this project automates at proxy or partial confidence and accepts the ceiling; here there is no mechanism to read, which makes this structure rather than effort.
Three observables were considered and rejected on principle, not cost. Counting the authorised set against a threshold would publish a number this project invented inside an OSCAL document citing an ASD control id. Observing egress from a proxy or CASB measures what access exists, not what is authorised, and its only detectable failure belongs to ism-1175. Reading an identity-governance campaign's completion records that a review happened, not that its outcome was proportionate.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The register of privileged user accounts explicitly authorised to access online services, recording for each account the services authorised, the business function requiring them, the approving authority and the date of the most recent proportionality review.

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: Both sides of the control's comparison are approval and judgement artefacts. The authorised population is defined by an approval decision rather than by any group membership that implements it, and "what a user's duties require" exists in no system as an attribute. No product implements the limitation the way a policy engine implements an authentication requirement, so there is no configuration state to read -- this is a gap no amount of engineering closes, not a collector nobody has written yet.

statements.description: Privileged user accounts explicitly authorised to access online services are strictly limited to only what is required for users to undertake their duties or functions.

components.title: Third Party Online Services
components.description: Assessment coverage provided by nobytes.compliance collectors and nobytes_cca evaluators for third-party-online-services. This document asserts what is ASSESSED, not what is implemented.

control-implementations.description: Controls this component can produce evidence for. A control absent from this list is not assessed on this platform.

implemented-requirements.description: Combines both barriers at once: the service belongs to a third party, and the people being authenticated are customers rather than staff. Neither the configuration nor the population appears anywhere in the estate this project can reach.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The third-party service register, for entries that handle sensitive customer data, recording the customer authentication arrangement agreed with the provider.

props.name: attestation-owner
props.value: Product owner for each customer-facing service, consolidated by the CISO function

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: The service is operated by a provider we do not control and authenticates a population of people who hold no account in our directory. There is no system of ours that could be queried to produce this evidence.

statements.description: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate human users to third-party online customer services that process, store or communicate their organisation’s sensitive customer data.

implemented-requirements.remarks: Residual assessment gap: Combines both barriers at once: the service belongs to a third party, and the people being authenticated are customers rather than staff. Neither the configuration nor the population appears anywhere in the estate this project can reach.

implemented-requirements.description: Same structural barrier as ism-1679, with an extra judgement no tool can make: "where available" requires establishing that a provider offers no multi-factor option at all. That is a statement about a product's feature set at a point in time, evidenced by the provider, not by our estate.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The third-party service register, recording for each non-sensitive-data service whether multi-factor authentication is offered by the provider and, where offered, that it is enabled.

props.name: attestation-owner
props.value: Service owner for each third-party arrangement, consolidated by the CISO function

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: The authentication configuration belongs to a provider we do not operate, and the "where available" qualifier additionally requires evidence about what a third-party product offers. Neither is present anywhere in our own systems, so no collector could be written that would answer this honestly.

statements.description: Multi-factor authentication (where available) is used to authenticate human users to third-party online services that process, store or communicate their organisation’s non-sensitive data.

implemented-requirements.remarks: Residual assessment gap: Same structural barrier as ism-1679, with an extra judgement no tool can make: "where available" requires establishing that a provider offers no multi-factor option at all. That is a statement about a product's feature set at a point in time, evidenced by the provider, not by our estate.

implemented-requirements.description: The control is fully addressed by the attestation, but only a human can make it. The subject is another organisation's identity system, and nothing in our estate holds its configuration. Reading our own tenant tells us how OUR staff authenticate to US, which is a different control (ism-1504) and must never be substituted for this one.

props.name: attestation-source
props.value: The register of third-party online services that process, store or communicate the organisation's sensitive data, recording the authentication arrangement agreed with each provider and the contractual clause requiring it.

props.name: attestation-owner
props.value: Service owner for each third-party arrangement, consolidated by the CISO function

props.name: why-not-observable
props.value: Multi-factor authentication here is enforced by a provider we do not operate, in a tenant we cannot query. There is no API, agent or log we could be entitled to that would reveal another organisation's authentication policy, so this is not a gap that engineering effort closes.

components.title: Windows Operating System
components.description: Assessment coverage provided by nobytes.compliance collectors and nobytes_cca evaluators for windows-operating-system. This document asserts what is ASSESSED, not what is implemented.

control-implementations.description: Controls this component can produce evidence for. A control absent from this list is not assessed on this platform.

implemented-requirements.description: The control names seven file types. AppLocker has five rule collections, and Microsoft documents what each covers: Executable (.exe, .com), Windows Installer (.msi, .mst, .msp), Scripts (.ps1, .bat, .cmd, .vbs, .js), DLLs (.dll, .ocx) and Packaged apps (.appx). Compiled HTML (.chm), HTML applications (.hta) and control panel applets (.cpl) appear in NO AppLocker rule collection, so an AppLocker-only estate cannot satisfy this control however well configured -- and an organisation that treats AppLocker as equivalent to ML1 application control has a gap it does not know about. Surfacing that is the point of this check. Where App Control for Business is enforcing instead, its code integrity rules are not readable from the collected state and the result is unassessed rather than a guess in either direction.

statements.description: Application control restricts the execution of executables, libraries, scripts, installers, compiled HTML, HTML applications and control panel applets to an organisation-approved set.

implemented-requirements.remarks: Residual assessment gap: The control names seven file types. implemented-requirements.description: Observes that an application control mechanism is in ENFORCING mode -- AppLocker with at least one rule collection set to Enabled, or App Control for Business running a code integrity policy. Two gaps are stated rather than hidden. "Implemented" is a judgement about an operational control, and a policy can enforce while permitting everything, so what is observed is enforcement mode rather than efficacy. And AuditOnly is deliberately not counted as implemented: an audit-mode collection writes an event and blocks nothing, which is the most likely way a workstation looks protected and is not.

statements.description: Application control is implemented on workstations.

implemented-requirements.remarks: Residual assessment gap: Observes that an application control mechanism is in ENFORCING mode -- AppLocker with at least one rule collection set to Enabled, or App Control for Business running a code integrity policy. Two gaps are stated rather than hidden. "Implemented" is a judgement about an operational control, and a policy can enforce while permitting everything, so what is observed is enforcement mode rather than efficacy. And AuditOnly is deliberately not counted as implemented: an audit-mode collection writes an event and blocks nothing, which is the most likely way a workstation looks protected and is not.

implemented-requirements.description:
This is the control AppLocker's default rules fail quietly. Those rules allow Everyone to execute anything under %WINDIR% and %PROGRAMFILES%; %WINDIR%\Temp is inside %WINDIR%, is the operating system's temporary folder, and is writable by standard users on a default install. So a host can enforce all five rule collections, report thousands of rules, and still let a standard user drop an executable into a temporary folder and run it. The check answers that by comparing the allow rules against the directories THIS host reports as writable by a non-administrator, rather than against a hardcoded list -- an estate that has hardened C:\Windows\Temp is in a different position from one that has not.
What it does not prove, in three parts. It enumerates a defined set of profile, operating-system, browser and email-client locations; a temporary folder belonging to some other installed application is outside what was probed, which is why confidence is partial and never direct. It reads DACLs rather than performing an access check, so ace ordering, inheritance and group nesting are simplified in the direction that over-reports. And it judges only rule collections that are ENFORCING: a collection left NotConfigured restricts nothing anywhere, which is ism-0843 and ism-1657's finding, and repeating it under every control it touches would bury the specific gap this check exists to surface.
An allow rule scoped to administrative principals is recorded but not counted as a failure here, because the control is about locations rather than about whether privileged accounts are themselves subject to application control. A deployment that reads it more strictly -- and at ML2/ML3 it probably should -- sets fail_on_administrator_allow.

implemented-requirements.description: The control is a binary state and both halves are directly observable: whether the optional feature is present, and whether policy disables the IE11 application. The one residual gap is IE mode inside Microsoft Edge, which is a deliberately supported configuration and is reported in the facts rather than judged, since the control speaks to Internet Explorer 11 as a browser rather than to the MSHTML engine.

statements.description: Internet Explorer 11 is disabled or removed.

implemented-requirements.remarks: Residual assessment gap: The control is a binary state and both halves are directly observable: whether the optional feature is present, and whether policy disables the IE11 application. The one residual gap is IE mode inside Microsoft Edge, which is a deliberately supported configuration and is reported in the facts rather than judged, since the control speaks to Internet Explorer 11 as a browser rather than to the MSHTML engine.

implemented-requirements.description: The control names six application families. The vendored end-of-life dataset covers Office productivity suites, two web browsers and Java; searching endoflife.date's 477-product index confirms it carries no entry for Microsoft Edge, any PDF reader, email clients or security products, and browser extensions are not an installed-application concept at all. Those gaps are named in every result rather than omitted, because "checked and supported" and "not checked at all" must not render the same way. Adobe Flash Player is judged from public record instead of a feed -- the control names it explicitly, Adobe ended support on 2020-12-31 and began blocking content on 2021-01-12, so any installation is unsupported without argument. An application that cannot be mapped to a support timeline is reported as unmapped and is neither passed nor failed; and where NOTHING could be mapped the result is unassessed rather than a vacuous pass. Support is judged as of the fact's collection date, so re-running over archived evidence reproduces the verdict that was true when it was gathered.
